source_text: Incipit a testimonio dei et merito fidei, cum dicimus, PATER QVI IN CAELIS ES. nam et deum oramus et fidem commendamus, cuius meritum est haec appellatio. scriptum est: qui in eum crediderint, dedit eis potestatem, ut filii dei uocentur. quamquam frequentissime dominus patrem nobis pronuntiauit deum, immo et praecepit, ne quem in terris patrem uocemus, nisi quem habemus in caelis. itaque sic adorantes etiam praeceptum obimus. felices, qui patrem agnoscunt. hoc est quod Israeli exprobratur, quod caelum ac terram spiritus contestatur, filios, dicens, genui, et illi me non agnouerunt. dicendo autem patrem deum quoque cognominamus. appellatio ista et pietatis et potestatis est. item in patre filius inuocatur. ego enim, inquit, et pater unum sumus. ne mater quidem ecclesia praeteritur. siquidem in filio et patre mater recognoscitur, de qua constat et patris et filii nomen. uno igitur genere aut uocabulo et deum cum suis honoramus et praecepti meminimus et oblitos patris - denotamus.
thought_title: The Father in heaven: faith, sonship, and the church as mother
orientation: Tertullian has just said the Lord's Prayer is a summary of the whole gospel, and now he begins expounding its first words, 'Our Father who art in heaven.'
pass_a_gloss: It begins from the testimony of God and the merit of faith, when we say, FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN. For we both pray to God and commend faith, whose merit is this address. It is written: to those who have believed in him, he gave them power, that they may be called sons of God. Although most frequently the Lord declared God to be Father to us, indeed he also commanded, that we call no one on earth father, except the one whom we have in heaven. And so, praying in this way, we also fulfill the command. Happy are those who acknowledge the Father. This is what is reproached to Israel, what the Spirit calls heaven and earth to witness, saying, I begot sons, and they did not know me. But by saying Father, we also name God. This address is both of piety and of power. Likewise in the Father the Son is invoked. For I, he says, and the Father are one. Not even mother church is passed over. Since in the Son and the Father the mother is recognized, from whom the name of both Father and Son is established. Therefore by one kind or one word we both honor God with his own, and remember the command, and mark those who have forgotten the Father.

choices.why: The first words of the Lord's Prayer as Tertullian quotes them; the archaic 'art' preserves the liturgical register of the Latin second-person singular.
Keeps the genitive relation explicit: the address 'Father' is the merit or deserving quality of faith, not merely a reward for faith.

choices.term: appellatio ista et pietatis et potestatis est
choices.english: This address is both of piety and of power
choices.why: The double genitive is preserved literally; 'address' renders appellatio as the act of naming God Father, not just a title.
rejected: This name belongs to both devotion and authority
This title is one of both love and power

choices.english: Not even mother church is passed over
choices.why: The word order and the emphatic 'ne...quidem' are kept; 'mother church' is the standard English rendering of mater ecclesia.
rejected: Mother Church is not omitted either
Even the church as mother is not left out

choices.english: we mark those who have forgotten the Father
choices.why: 'Mark' renders denotamus in its sense of pointing out or branding, which fits Tertullian's polemical edge against Israel.
rejected: we denounce those who forgot the Father
we point out those who have forgotten the Father

pass_b_english: It begins with God's own testimony and the merit of faith when we say, "Father who art in heaven." For we both pray to God and commend faith, whose merit is this very address. It is written: "To those who believed in him he gave the power to be called children of God" (John 1:12). Yet the Lord very often declared God to be our Father, and indeed commanded that we call no one on earth father, except the one we have in heaven (Matthew 23:9). So when we pray in this way, we are also carrying out a command. Happy are those who acknowledge the Father.

This is what Israel is reproached for, what the Spirit testifies to heaven and earth: "I begot children," he says, "and they did not know me" (Isaiah 1:2). And when we say Father, we also name God. This address is both of piety and of power. In the Father, the Son is also invoked. "For I and the Father are one," he says (John 10:30). Not even mother church is passed over. For in the Son and the Father the mother is recognized, from whom the name of both Father and Son is established. So with one word or name we honor God together with his own, remember the command, and mark those who have forgotten the Father.

problems.quote: what the Spirit calls heaven and earth to witness
problems.why: Agency reversed; the spirit testifies to heaven and earth, not calls them to witness.
problems.fix: what the Spirit testifies to heaven and earth
problems.ruling: "spiritus contestatur" = the Spirit bears witness to heaven and earth; English reverses agency, making heaven/earth witnesses rather than recipients of testimony.

problems.quote: "I begot children," he says, "and they did not know me" (Isaiah 1:2)
problems.source_quote: genui, et illi me non agnouerunt
problems.why: The Latin passage does not cite Isaiah 1:2; the quoted words are not from that verse.
problems.fix: Quote without the incorrect citation or replace with the correct reference (e.g., Isaiah 43:10) if known.
problems.ruling: Isaiah 1:2 says 'rebelled', not 'did not know me'; the Latin 'me non agnouerunt' matches no single verse, likely conflating Isaiah 1:2 with Deuteronomy 32.
